p-12.1-outputs-table.title: 12.1 Plan Procurement Management (continued): document updates, OPA updates, Table 12-1 comparison of procurement documentation
p-12.1-outputs-table.notes: Document updates: lessons learned (regulations and compliance, data gathering and analysis, source selection); milestone list (when sellers deliver); requirements documentation (technical and contractual/legal requirements); RTM; risk register (each approved seller brings unique risks depending on its organisation, contract duration, external environment, delivery method, contract type and agreed price); stakeholder register (regulators, contracting and legal personnel). OPA updates: information on qualified sellers. Simple projects may combine outputs; complex, contractor-heavy projects need several document types. Table 12-1 (representative, not prescriptive - organisation, environment and law dictate documents): procurement management plan - coordination and integration with other project work (resources, schedule, budget), timetable of key activities, procurement metrics, stakeholder responsibilities, assumptions and constraints, legal jurisdiction and payment currency, independent estimates, risk management issues, prequalified sellers; procurement strategy - delivery methods, type of agreements, procurement phases; statement of work - description of the procurement item, specifications, quality requirements and performance metrics, collateral services, acceptance methods and criteria, performance data and reports required, quality, period and place of performance, currency and payment schedule, warranty; bid documents - RFI, RFQ, RFP.

p-12.2-conduct-procurements.title: 12.2 Conduct Procurements: seller proposals, advertising, bidder conferences, proposal evaluation, negotiation, selected sellers, agreement components
p-12.2-conduct-procurements.notes: Obtain seller responses, select a seller and award a contract; key benefit: a qualified seller is selected and the legal agreement for delivery implemented; end results are established agreements including formal contracts; performed periodically as needed. Inputs: plan (scope management plan incl. seller scope; requirements management plan incl. how sellers manage their requirements; communications management plan - buyer-seller communication; risk management plan; procurement management plan; configuration management plan - how sellers provide configuration management consistent with the buyer; cost baseline - procurement budget and costs of managing the process and sellers); documents (lessons learned, project schedule - procurement activities and contractor due dates, requirements documentation, risk register, stakeholder register); procurement documentation (written record used to reach the agreement: bid documents - RFI, RFP, RFQ; procurement SOW - goals, requirements, outcomes for a quantifiable response; independent cost estimates - reasonableness check; source selection criteria with weights; the buyer may contract more than one seller to mitigate single-seller risk); seller proposals (basis for the evaluation body; good practice: price proposal separate from technical proposal; evaluated against source selection criteria to choose the seller best satisfying requirements); EEFs (procurement laws and local-seller requirements, external economy, marketplace, past seller experience, prior agreements, contract management systems); OPAs (prequalified preferred sellers, selection policies, agreement templates and guidelines, invoicing and payment policies). Tools: expert judgment (proposal evaluation, technical subject matter, finance, engineering, design, development, supply chain, regulatory environment, laws and compliance, negotiation); advertising (expand seller lists through general or trade publications; most government jurisdictions require public advertising or online posting); bidder conferences (also contractor, vendor or pre-bid conferences; buyer meets prospective sellers before proposals to ensure a clear, common understanding and no preferential treatment); data analysis - proposal evaluation (complete, fully responsive to bid documents, SOW, criteria); interpersonal skills - negotiation (clarify structure, rights, obligations and terms before signing; final language reflects all agreements; ends with a signed contract; led by a procurement team member with signing authority; PM and team may attend to assist). Outputs: selected sellers (in a competitive range from evaluation; complex, high-value, high-risk procurements generally need senior management approval before award); agreements (contract = mutually binding agreement obligating the seller to provide specified products/services/results and the buyer to compensate, a legal relationship subject to remedy in the courts; components may include: SOW or major deliverables; schedule, milestones or required schedule date; performance reporting; pricing and payment terms; inspection, quality and acceptance criteria; warranty and future support; incentives and penalties; insurance and performance bonds; subcontractor approvals; general terms and conditions; change request handling; termination clause and alternative dispute resolution); change requests; plan updates (requirements, quality, communications, risk, procurement management plans; scope, schedule, cost baselines - e.g., seller delivery changes or fluctuating material and labour prices); document updates (lessons learned, requirements documentation, RTM, resource calendars - seller availability, risk register, stakeholder register); OPA updates (prospective and prequalified seller lists; experience with sellers). Data flow (Figure 12-5, verified): inputs from plan, documents, procurement documentation, enterprise and sellers (seller proposals); outputs - selected sellers to 12.3; change requests to 4.6; agreements to 4.1, 4.5, 4.7, 6.5, 7.3, 9.6, 12.3, 13.1 and 13.2. Source note: Figure 12-5 does not list 5.2 Collect Requirements or 11.2 Identify Risks, although their own data flow diagrams (Figures 5-5 and 11-7) show agreements received from 12.2 - lessons note the inconsistency.

p-12.3-control-procurements.title: 12.3 Control Procurements: contract administration, payments linked to work, claims administration, inspections, audits, closed procurements
p-12.3-control-procurements.notes: Manage procurement relationships, monitor contract performance, make changes and corrections, close out contracts; key benefit: both seller's and buyer's performance meet requirements under the legal agreement; performed throughout as needed. Both buyer and seller administer the contract to meet obligations and protect rights; be aware of legal implications of actions; on multi-provider projects manage communication among providers; many organisations treat contract administration as a separate organisational function (procurement administrator may sit on the team but report elsewhere). Integrates project management processes with contractual relationships at multiple levels. Administrative activities: collect data and keep detailed physical and financial performance records with measurable procurement performance indicators; refine procurement plans and schedules; gather, analyse and report procurement data; monitor the procurement environment; pay invoices. Quality of controls - independence and credibility of procurement audits - is critical; the code of ethics, legal counsel and anti-corruption initiatives help. Financial component: monitor payments so terms are met and compensation is linked to progress; payments should closely match work accomplished; contracts tying payment to outputs and deliverables rather than inputs such as labour hours have better controls. Agreements can be amended any time before closure by mutual consent per the change control terms, typically in writing. Inputs: plan (requirements management plan, risk management plan - seller-created risk activities, procurement management plan, change management plan - seller-created changes, schedule baseline); documents (assumption log, lessons learned, milestone list, quality reports - seller non-compliance, requirements documentation, RTM, risk register, stakeholder register - contracted members, sellers, contracting officers); agreements (verify terms are met); procurement documentation (SOW, payment information, contractor performance information, plans, drawings, correspondence); approved change requests (modifications to terms, SOW, pricing, descriptions; all procurement changes documented in writing and approved before implementation through this process; seller changes may affect other sellers); work performance data (seller technical performance, activity status, costs incurred or committed, invoices paid); EEFs (contract change control system, marketplace, financial management and accounts payable system, the buyer's code of ethics); OPAs (procurement policies). Tools: expert judgment (functional areas, laws and compliance, claims administration); claims administration (contested changes and potential constructive changes - where buyer and seller cannot agree on compensation or that a change occurred - are claims; unresolved claims become disputes and then appeals; documented, processed, monitored and managed per contract terms; if unresolved by the parties, alternative dispute resolution (ADR) per contract procedures; negotiated settlement is preferred); data analysis - performance reviews (quality, resource, schedule and cost performance against the agreement), earned value analysis (SV, CV, SPI, CPI for degree of variance), trend analysis (forecast EAC to see if performance is improving or deteriorating); inspection (structured review of contractor work, from deliverable reviews to physical site walkthroughs by buyer and contractor); audits (structured review of the procurement process; audit rights and obligations described in the contract; observations to both PMs). Outputs: closed procurements (buyer, usually via its authorised procurement administrator, gives the seller formal written notice of completion; closure requirements are in the contract terms and procurement plan; typically all deliverables on time and meeting requirements, no outstanding claims or invoices, all final payments made, deliverables approved by the PM team); work performance information (deliverables received, technical performance achieved, costs incurred and accepted vs the SOW budget); procurement documentation updates (contract and schedules, requested unapproved changes, approved changes, seller technical documentation, deliverables, seller performance reports and warranties, invoices and payment records, inspection results); change requests (incl. requested but unresolved changes - buyer direction or seller action the other party considers a constructive change; uniquely identified and documented in correspondence because they may lead to claims); plan updates (risk management plan, procurement management plan, schedule baseline - incl. cascading seller delays affecting other sellers, cost baseline); document updates (lessons learned incl. claims to avoid recurrence, resource requirements, RTM - satisfied requirements, risk register, stakeholder register - changing contractors); OPA updates (payment schedules and requests per contract terms; seller performance evaluation documentation - ability to continue, eligibility for future work, ratings; prequalified seller list updates - sellers may be removed for poor performance; lessons learned repository - actual vs projected results of the procurement; procurement file - complete indexed contract documentation incl. the closed contract for the final project files). Data flow (Figure 12-7, verified): approved change requests from 4.6; WPD from 4.3; procurement documentation from 12.1; agreements from 12.2; outputs - closed procurements and documentation updates to the procurement documentation store; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.

h-stakeholder-intro.title: Project Stakeholder Management: purpose and four processes
h-stakeholder-intro.notes: Identify the people, groups or organisations that could impact or be impacted by the project, analyse expectations and impact, and develop strategies to engage stakeholders in decisions and execution. Processes: 13.1 Identify Stakeholders (identify stakeholders regularly and analyse and document their interests, involvement, interdependencies, influence and potential impact on success); 13.2 Plan Stakeholder Engagement (develop approaches to involve stakeholders based on needs, expectations, interests and potential impact); 13.3 Manage Stakeholder Engagement (communicate and work with stakeholders to meet needs and expectations, address issues and foster appropriate engagement); 13.4 Monitor Stakeholder Engagement (monitor relationships and tailor engagement strategies by modifying strategies and plans). (Overview continues on PDF 541.)
